analogy.p: Imagine building a heated house on a frozen lake. The ice looks solid, but the heat from inside melts it from below until the house tilts and sinks. To avoid this you would lift the house on stilts and insulate the floor, which costs a lot. That is the permafrost problem in Alaska. The analogy breaks down because permafrost is soil and ice rather than a lake, and because the Arctic climate is warming, so the ground is thawing even without buildings.
analogy.t: Building a house on a frozen lake

bullets: **Development** means using the resources of a place (energy, minerals, fish, scenery) to create jobs, money and better living standards.
**Push and pull logic:** resources elsewhere are running out (push), while cold regions hold large untapped reserves (pull).
**Technology** such as insulated pipelines, ice-strengthened ships and heated buildings has made development possible.
**Extreme environment** means a place with harsh conditions (very low temperatures, strong winds, darkness, permafrost) that make human activity difficult and costly.
Cold environments cover roughly a fifth of the Earth's land surface, so the resources they hold matter globally.
Governments often support development to gain **energy security** and tax income, not only company profit.
Always link a point to the **extreme environment**: marks are awarded for explaining why the cold makes something an opportunity or a problem.
core.h: Why cold environments are being developed
core.p: Cold environments (the polar regions and tundra) were once left almost untouched because they were too remote, too cold and too expensive to reach. Today the picture is changing. Global demand for **oil, gas and minerals** keeps rising, easily reached supplies elsewhere are being used up, and **new technology** now lets companies work in extreme conditions. Warming in the Arctic is also melting sea ice, which makes some areas easier to reach by ship. The specification asks you to know a **case study of a cold environment** to show the **development opportunities** and the **challenges** of developing an extreme environment. In this note the case study is **Alaska, USA**.

bullets: **Location:** north-west corner of North America; the North Slope borders the Arctic Ocean, and the south coast (e.g. Valdez) borders the Gulf of Alaska.

**Climate of the North Slope (e.g. Utqiagvik):** monthly mean temperatures are below 0 degrees Celsius for about nine months; January is around minus 25 degrees Celsius and July only about 4 degrees Celsius.
**Precipitation** is very low (roughly 100 to 150 mm a year), so the tundra is sometimes called a 'cold desert'; the ground stays wet in summer only because permafrost stops drainage.
**Daylight:** in midwinter the sun does not rise for more than two months (polar night) and in summer it does not set for about eighty days (midnight sun).
**Population:** low density; many remote communities, including Alaska Native peoples such as the Inupiat, who traditionally hunt, fish and whale for food (subsistence).
**Why it is a good case study:** it shows both big economic opportunities and serious physical, environmental and social challenges.
In answers, give **place-specific detail** (Prudhoe Bay, Trans-Alaska Pipeline, Valdez, Denali, Red Dog mine) because generic answers are capped at lower marks.
core.p: Alaska is the largest US state and lies in the far north-west of North America, with its northern edge on the Arctic Ocean. It has a very small population for its size (well under a million people), most living in the south around Anchorage. The northern area, the **North Slope**, has a **tundra climate**: winters are long, dark and extremely cold and summers are short and cool. The ground is **permafrost** (permanently frozen) with only a thin **active layer** that thaws in summer. Alaska is a good case study because it has all four main types of development: **oil and gas, minerals, fishing and tourism**.

bullets: **Discovery:** Prudhoe Bay oilfield, found 1968, is the largest oilfield in North America.
**Transport:** the Trans-Alaska Pipeline carries oil about 1,300 km south to **Valdez**, which stays free of ice all year, so tankers can load in winter.
**Jobs:** direct jobs in drilling and pipeline maintenance, plus indirect jobs in catering, transport and construction (the **multiplier effect**).
**Government income:** taxes and royalties from oil help pay for schools, hospitals and roads; the **Alaska Permanent Fund** (set up 1976) invests oil money and pays a yearly dividend to residents.
**Infrastructure:** oil companies built roads, airstrips, power supplies and communications that also benefit local communities.
**Energy security:** supplies the USA with its own oil rather than relying on imports.
**Gas:** large natural gas reserves are also present, though transporting gas is harder than oil.
**Evaluation point:** oil revenue has fluctuated with world oil prices, so relying on one resource is risky (boom and bust).
core.p: The biggest development in Alaska is **oil**. Huge reserves were found at **Prudhoe Bay** on the North Slope in 1968. To move the oil to the ice-free port of **Valdez** in the south, the **Trans-Alaska Pipeline System (TAPS)** was built between 1974 and 1977. It is about 1,300 km (800 miles) long. Oil extraction brings very large income to the state, funds public services and supports thousands of jobs, so it is the main economic opportunity in the region.

bullets: **Red Dog mine:** a zinc and lead mine in north-west Alaska, operated with the local Alaska Native regional corporation (NANA), providing well-paid jobs and income for local people.
**Gold** and other metals are mined in the interior, often using seasonal operations in the short warmer season.
**Local benefits:** wages, training and royalty payments go to communities, helping reduce poverty in isolated villages.
**National benefits:** minerals are exported, helping the trade balance and supplying industry.
**Extreme environment factor:** frozen ground can make digging harder in winter, but some ore is mined from open pits whose haul roads are built on frozen ground.
**Disadvantage:** mine waste (tailings) and dust can pollute streams and tundra, and mining scars the landscape.
**Limitation:** the mines are remote, so concentrate must be transported long distances to ports, adding cost.
core.p: Alaska is rich in minerals including **zinc, lead, gold, silver and coal**. The best known is the **Red Dog mine** in the north-west, one of the world's largest sources of zinc. Mining brings jobs and income to remote areas where there are few other employers. However, mineral extraction needs roads, power and ports, which is difficult and costly in cold environments, and waste must be stored carefully.

bullets: **Why so many fish:** upwelling of cold water brings nutrients to the surface, causing plankton blooms that support food chains.
**Main species:** salmon (sockeye, pink, chum), Alaska pollock, Pacific cod, halibut and king crab.
**Jobs:** fishing crews, processing factories (often seasonal), boat building and ports.
**Exports:** frozen and canned fish sold worldwide, bringing in foreign income.
**Subsistence fishing** also provides food for Alaska Native communities.
**Challenge:** storms, ice and freezing sea spray make fishing among the most dangerous jobs in the world.
**Sustainability:** fishing needs quotas to prevent overfishing (see the management note).
core.p: Alaska's cold, nutrient-rich seas, especially the **Bering Sea** and **Gulf of Alaska**, support huge fish stocks, including **salmon, pollock, cod and crab**. Commercial fishing is one of the largest private employers and Alaska lands a very large share of the wild fish caught in the USA. Fishing also supports processing plants and exports. Cold water holds more dissolved oxygen and supports plenty of plankton, which is the base of the food chain, so fish stocks can be very productive.

bullets: **Attractions:** Denali (Mount Denali, about 6,190 m), glaciers, whale watching, bear viewing, northern lights, Iditarod dog sled race.
**Season:** most tourists come in the short summer when it is lighter and warmer, so jobs are seasonal.
**Jobs:** guides, hotel and restaurant staff, pilots, boat operators; tourism income spreads to local shops and services.
**Cruise ships** bring many visitors to coastal towns, but numbers can overwhelm small places.
**Winter tourism** (northern lights, skiing, dog sledding) is growing, which helps spread the season.
**Link to extreme environment:** the very qualities that cause problems (cold, remoteness, wilderness) become the tourist attraction.
**Downside:** visitors cause litter, trampling of tundra, wildlife disturbance and carbon emissions from flights and ships.
core.p: Tourism is Alaska's second major opportunity. Visitors come for **wilderness, wildlife, glaciers, mountains and the northern lights**. Attractions include **Denali National Park** (home to the highest mountain in North America), **Glacier Bay**, wildlife viewing of bears, whales and caribou, cruise ships and adventure activities such as dog sledding, kayaking and fishing. Tourism creates jobs without extracting a resource that runs out, but it is **seasonal** and can damage fragile ecosystems.

bullets: **Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act 1971:** settled land claims and created Native corporations, giving communities a stake in development.
**Services:** schools, health clinics, airports and power plants in remote villages are partly funded from resource income.
**Employment:** development offers jobs in an area where traditional hunting offers little cash income.
**Permanent Fund Dividend:** every eligible resident receives a yearly payment from oil investments.
**Skills and training:** workers gain technical skills which they can use elsewhere.
**Uneven benefits:** many specialist workers are brought in from outside, so local people may not get the best jobs.
**Cost of living:** supplies are flown or shipped in, so food and fuel cost more, which cancels out part of the higher wages.
core.h: Social and economic benefits to people of Alaska
core.p: Alongside the four industries, development can improve life for local people. After the oil discovery, Alaska Native peoples gained rights and money through the **Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (1971)**, which created native corporations that own land and run businesses. Money from resources has paid for services in remote places. But benefits are uneven: some communities gain jobs and income, while others see little benefit and bear the costs.

bullets: **Equipment problems:** metals can become brittle, fuel and oil can thicken or freeze, batteries lose power, and machines need heated garages or special lubricants.
**Short working season:** outdoor construction can only be done in the few warmer months, or in winter on frozen ground, so projects take longer and cost more.
**Health and safety:** risk of **frostbite** and **hypothermia**; workers need rotas, insulated clothing and shelters.
**Wind chill and blizzards** can shut roads and airstrips for days.
**Darkness:** polar night means artificial lighting is needed and can affect mental health (seasonal depression).
**Heating costs:** buildings need a lot of energy and insulation, increasing the cost of every project.
**Impact on production:** oil can still be produced in winter, but maintenance and repairs are harder.
core.p: The cold is the first challenge. Temperatures on the North Slope are below freezing for most of the year, with winter lows below minus 40 degrees Celsius in places. Machinery, vehicles and pipes are all affected. Workers need protective clothing, heated shelters and frequent breaks, which reduces productivity and raises costs. Strong winds create wind chill and blizzards. Long periods of darkness add to the difficulty and affect people's wellbeing.

bullets: **Active layer:** the thin top layer of soil that thaws in summer and freezes in winter; water cannot drain through the frozen layer beneath, so the tundra becomes boggy.
**Problem:** melting causes **subsidence**, damaging foundations, roads, airstrips and pipelines.
**Solution 1 - stilts:** buildings and pipelines are raised on stilts so heat does not pass into the ground and air can circulate underneath.
**Solution 2 - gravel pads:** thick layers of gravel insulate the permafrost under roads and drilling sites.
**Solution 3 - thermosyphons:** metal heat pipes in the support posts carry heat out of the ground to keep it frozen.
**Solution 4 - insulation:** pipes are wrapped in insulation, and buildings have well-insulated floors.
**Solution 5 - ice roads and ice pads:** built in winter from compacted snow and water to protect the tundra and then melt in spring.
**Climate change** is now warming the Arctic faster than the global average and thawing permafrost, increasing the risk further.
core.h: Challenge 2: permafrost and building on frozen ground
core.p: **Permafrost** is ground that stays frozen all year. It is strong when frozen, but if heat reaches it, it melts and the ground becomes soft and unstable. Heat from warm buildings, pipelines (oil in the pipeline is warm), roads and machinery can melt it. When it melts, the ground **subsides** (sinks) and buildings tilt, pipes crack and roads buckle. This makes construction in Alaska much more expensive and needs special engineering.

bullets: **Length:** about 1,300 km (800 miles) from Prudhoe Bay to Valdez.
**Above-ground sections** (about half) sit on vertical support members to keep heat away from permafrost.
**Thermosyphons (radiators)** on the supports keep the ground below frozen.
**Zig-zag design:** allows expansion, contraction and ground movement in earthquakes.
**Insulation:** keeps oil warm enough to flow while limiting heat loss.
**Animal crossings:** raised sections or burial let caribou pass.
**Dalton Highway** was built alongside to carry supplies and workers, opening up the interior.
**Evaluation:** engineering solutions are expensive and show the extra cost of developing cold environments.
core.h: Case study example: Trans-Alaska Pipeline design
core.p: The Trans-Alaska Pipeline shows how engineers solved the problems of a cold environment. Because the oil leaves the ground warm, a buried pipe would thaw the permafrost, so around half of the pipeline is built **above ground** on supports with thermosyphons. Where the ground is stable or not ice-rich, it is buried. The pipe is built in a **zig-zag** to allow it to expand and contract with temperature changes and to move during earthquakes. Raised sections and underground crossings allow **caribou** to migrate.

bullets: **Few roads:** the Dalton Highway (about 667 km) is the only road to the North Slope; much of the state has no road network.
**Transport costs:** air freight and barge deliveries make food, fuel and building materials expensive.
**Frozen seas:** northern ports are blocked by sea ice for most of the year; ice roads are only usable in winter.
**Small local workforce:** low population means skilled workers are flown in on rotation shifts, which costs money.
**Distance from markets:** exports must travel long distances.
**Emergency response:** spills, accidents or medical emergencies take longer to reach.
**Infrastructure needs:** developing resources requires building roads, airports, power plants and housing from scratch.
core.p: Much of Alaska is far from large cities and has very few roads. The North Slope is more than 1,000 km from the nearest large city, and many communities can only be reached by **air or by boat** or on **ice roads** in winter. This means supplies, fuel and workers must be flown or shipped in at great cost. Ports in the north are frozen for much of the year, so deliveries are only possible in a short summer window. Remote locations also make emergency help slow and the workforce small.

bullets: **Oil spills:** harm wildlife, coat feathers and fur, and damage food chains; cold temperatures slow natural breakdown.
**Habitat loss and fragmentation:** roads, pipelines and drilling pads break up habitats and can block caribou migration.
**Slow recovery:** short growing season means vegetation takes decades to regrow after damage.
**Pollution:** waste, noise, air pollution from engines and gas flaring.
**Thawing permafrost** releases greenhouse gases, adding to global warming.
**Wildlife disturbance:** noise and traffic can disturb breeding of birds, polar bears and caribou.
**Mining waste** can contaminate rivers where salmon spawn.
**Climate change** driven partly by burning the oil extracted makes the problem worse.
core.p: Tundra ecosystems are fragile. Plants grow very slowly in the short, cold growing season, and decomposition is slow, so damage lasts for decades. Tyre tracks across tundra can leave scars for many years. The greatest risk is an **oil spill**. In 1989 the tanker **Exxon Valdez** ran aground in Prince William Sound, spilling about 11 million US gallons (roughly 40 million litres) of crude oil, killing huge numbers of seabirds, sea otters and fish and harming fishing communities. In cold water oil breaks down slowly, so the damage is long lasting.

bullets: **Subsistence lifestyle:** hunting and fishing provide food and are central to culture; disturbance of animals threatens both.
**Cultural change:** young people may move away from traditional lifestyles toward wage employment.
**Conflicts of interest:** companies and governments want income; some communities want to protect their land and wildlife.
**Boom and bust:** towns that grow with a resource boom can decline when prices fall.
**Social problems:** rapid change has been linked to social problems in some communities.
**Consultation:** local people should be consulted, and Native corporations give a voice in decisions.
**Mixed views:** use phrases like 'some local people...whereas others...' in evaluation answers.
core.p: Development also affects the people who already live in cold environments. Indigenous peoples such as the Inupiat rely on hunting caribou, fishing and whaling for food and for their culture. Oil and gas activity can disturb or move animals, and spills or pollution threaten food supplies. The arrival of outside workers and money can change traditional ways of life. Some people welcome the jobs and services; others fear losing their culture and land.

bullets: **Economic benefits** are large and quick (oil revenue, jobs) but depend on world prices and can run out.
**Environmental costs** are long term and may be irreversible, especially after a spill.
**Technology** (stilts, thermosyphons, double-hulled tankers) reduces but does not remove risk.
**Who benefits?** governments, companies and some local people; **who loses?** wildlife and communities dependent on subsistence.
**Short vs long term:** jobs now versus damage for future generations.
**Scale matters:** large projects such as oil drilling have bigger impacts than small tourism projects.
**Judgement phrase:** 'Overall, development is worthwhile only if it is carefully managed because...'
core.h: Evaluating development: weighing opportunities against challenges
core.p: Exam questions often ask you to **assess** or **evaluate** whether development is worthwhile. To score highly you must show both sides, link them to the extreme environment, and then give a **justified judgement**. Consider who benefits, who loses, and short term compared with long term. You can also judge how far technology can reduce the environmental risks.

bullets: **Climate change:** permafrost thaw releases methane and carbon dioxide, a positive feedback.
**Resource management:** fossil fuels are non-renewable; sustainable alternatives include renewable energy.
**Rainforests:** like Amazonia, cold environments face conflict between development and conservation.
**Hot deserts:** desert development also needs expensive technology (irrigation).
**Urban and economic topics:** the multiplier effect and uneven development apply here.
**Sustainable management (next note):** how development can be balanced with protecting the environment.
core.p: The Alaska case study connects to several other parts of your course. It links to **climate change** (burning fossil fuels raises temperatures and Arctic warming thaws permafrost), to **resource management** (oil as a non-renewable resource) and to **other ecosystems** (hot desert and rainforest development have similar conflicts between economy and environment). Making these links in a 9-mark answer shows depth.

exam: 'Give' or 'State' (1 mark): one fact such as 'Prudhoe Bay' or 'zinc'. No explanation needed.
'Describe' (2 to 3 marks): say what and where with named details, e.g. 'a 1,300 km pipeline runs from Prudhoe Bay to Valdez, partly on stilts'.
'Explain' (4 marks): two developed points, each as point + because + so. Example: 'Buildings are raised on stilts (1) because heat would melt permafrost (1) causing subsidence (1)'.
'Suggest' (usually 2 to 4 marks): apply your knowledge to the data given; use cautious language like 'could' and 'may'.
'Assess' or 'Evaluate' (6 or 9 marks): put opportunities and challenges together, use case study facts, and finish with a justified judgement; plan with a short list first.
'To what extent' questions need a balanced answer and a clear verdict, not just a list of ideas.
Use a **named case study** in every extended answer: the examiners reward place-specific facts and figures.
For climate graphs: quote temperatures with units, identify the highest and lowest and the range, and state how many months are below 0 degrees Celsius.
Use geographical terms (permafrost, active layer, subsidence, subsistence, multiplier effect) in the correct context.
Link back to the question: finish every paragraph with a sentence that answers 'so what?' for the command word used.

mistakes.r: Link a specific effect: for example, permafrost melts under heated buildings and pipelines, causing subsidence, so stilts and gravel pads are needed, which raises costs.
mistakes.w: Alaska is hard to develop because it is cold.

mistakes.r: Permafrost is permanently frozen ground (soil, rock and ice) below a thin active layer that thaws in summer.
mistakes.w: Permafrost is just frozen water on the surface.

mistakes.r: It is raised because warm oil would melt permafrost and the ground would subside.
mistakes.w: The pipeline is above ground because it is easier to build.

mistakes.r: Give both sides: jobs, tax and services, versus spill risk, habitat loss and boom and bust.
Use named detail: Prudhoe Bay, Valdez, Red Dog, Denali, Exxon Valdez 1989, Dalton Highway.
Tourists come for wilderness, wildlife, glaciers and northern lights; the extreme environment is the attraction, but also the limit.
mistakes.w: Tourists come because it is cold.

mistakes.r: Arctic is ocean surrounded by land; Antarctica is a continent. Alaska is an Arctic/tundra case study.
mistakes.w: The Arctic and Antarctic are the same.

mistakes.r: Use point, explain (because), and develop (so, which leads to), and link to extreme conditions.

summary: You must know a case study of a cold environment (Alaska) to show the opportunities for development (oil and gas, minerals, fishing, tourism) and the challenges of extreme temperatures, permafrost, inaccessibility and environmental and social impact. It matters because case-study detail and an evaluative judgement are what earn top marks in extended answers.

terms.d: Using resources and improving the economy and living standards of a place.
A place with harsh conditions such as very low temperatures, darkness or strong winds that make human activity difficult.
Ground that remains frozen for at least two consecutive years, often permanently.
The thin top layer of soil that thaws in summer and refreezes in winter above the permafrost.
The sinking of ground, often when permafrost thaws, damaging buildings and pipes.
Treeless cold environment with low-growing plants, short growing season and permafrost.
About 1,300 km oil pipeline from Prudhoe Bay to Valdez, built 1974-77 and partly raised on stilts.
A heat pipe in a support post that moves heat out of the ground to keep permafrost frozen.
Extra jobs and income created in other sectors when an industry brings wages into an area.
Hunting, fishing and gathering to feed your own household rather than for sale.
A wild area little changed by people and often valued for its scenery and wildlife.
Rapid growth when a resource is in demand followed by decline when prices or supplies fall.
Difficult to reach because of distance, lack of roads or ice.
The effect of wind making the air feel colder than the measured temperature.
1989 oil tanker disaster in Prince William Sound that spilled about 11 million US gallons of crude oil.

worked.ans: In Alaska, permafrost is a challenge because heat from buildings and the warm oil pipeline can melt the frozen ground (1), causing subsidence so foundations and pipes crack (1); engineers must use stilts and gravel pads, which raises costs. Inaccessibility is another challenge because the North Slope has only one road, the Dalton Highway, and ports are frozen for most of the year (1), so supplies and workers have to be flown in, which makes everything expensive (1). (4 marks)
worked.q: Explain two challenges of developing a cold environment you have studied. (4 marks)
steps: Choose two different challenges: permafrost and inaccessibility.
For each write point, then because, then so (consequence).

worked.ans: Alaska offers large opportunities. Oil from Prudhoe Bay is piped 1,300 km to Valdez, creating jobs and tax income that pays for services and the Permanent Fund dividend. Fishing in the Bering Sea and tourism at Denali add jobs and exports. However, there are serious challenges. Permafrost melts under heat so pipelines are put on stilts with thermosyphons, which raises costs. The area is remote with one road, so supplies are expensive. The Exxon Valdez spill in 1989 showed how an accident can damage wildlife and fishing for years in cold water where oil breaks down slowly. Overall, the opportunities are significant, especially for the economy, but because the environment is fragile and mistakes last a long time, development is only worthwhile if it is carefully managed. (6 marks: balanced, named detail, justified conclusion)
worked.q: Assess the opportunities and challenges of developing a cold environment you have studied. (6 marks)
steps: Plan: opportunities (oil, fishing, tourism), challenges (permafrost, remote, spills).
